name: Ancient Greek religion
areas: tablets at Knossos and Pylos name Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus
the last pagans, until Justinian's laws
the Greek cities of western Asia Minor
Greek cults in the cities of the Seleucid kings
routes: Colonists carry their gods to Italy and Sicily (from the 8th century BCE)
Alexander's conquests carry Greek cults to Egypt
marks: Linear B tablets here and at Pylos record offerings to Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus (14th–13th centuries BCE).
The oracle of Zeus at Dodona, the oldest in Greece by Herodotus's account.
The first Olympic Games were held in honour of Zeus in 776 BCE, by tradition; the last ancient Games in 393.
The oracle of Apollo, consulted by Greeks from the 8th century BCE until the end of the 4th century CE.
The Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone were celebrated here for about a thousand years, until the sanctuary was sacked in 396.
The temple of Artemis, rebuilt in the 6th century BCE, one of the Seven Wonders.
Pheidias's gold and ivory statue of Athena was dedicated in the Parthenon in 438 BCE.
Justinian forbade pagans to teach in 529, and the Platonic school of Athens closed.
notes: Mycenaean palaces at Knossos and Pylos record offerings to Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus on their Linear B tablets.
The Mycenaean palaces fall; the worship of the gods continues in the villages and sanctuaries of the Greek Dark Age.
The first Olympic Games honour Zeus (776 BCE, by tradition); the oracle of Delphi gains fame; colonists carry the gods to Italy and Sicily.
Homer's epics and Hesiod's Theogony give the gods their classic form; Greek colonies spread from the Black Sea to Massalia.
Great stone temples rise, such as Artemis's at Ephesus; the Mysteries of Eleusis draw initiates from all Greece.
Athens dedicates the Parthenon (438 BCE) and stages tragedies at the festival of Dionysus.
Socrates is condemned to death for impiety (399 BCE); Alexander's conquests carry Greek gods and temples to Egypt and Asia.
Greek cults spread through the Hellenistic kingdoms; the Romans identify their own gods with the Olympians.
Rome conquers Greece (146 BCE); the sanctuaries continue under Roman rule.
Hadrian completes the temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens (131–132); Pausanias describes the sanctuaries of Greece.
Theodosius bans all pagan sacrifice and worship (392); the last ancient Olympic Games are held (393, by tradition), and Eleusis is sacked (396).
Pagan philosophers still teach in Athens; temples are closed, destroyed or turned into churches.
Justinian forbids pagans to teach (529), and the Platonic school of Athens closes.
src: Simon Price, Religions of the Ancient Greeks (1999)
Jon D. Mikalson, Ancient Greek Religion (2nd ed., 2010)
